The experiments were performed at JET with mixed H-D plasmas and varying NBI and gas-puff sources.
The core Deuterium density was derived from the neutron rate, with around 80% of the neutrons originating from the ρ < 0.5 region.
The edge composition was measured by comparing the relative amplitude of Balmer Hα and Dα spectral lines.
The effective electron particle diffusion coefficient D_e was expected to lie within 0.2χ_eff < D_e < 0.6χ_eff based on previous studies.
The previous experimental analysis indicated a disparity in magnitude between the ion and electron particle transport coefficients, with D_i/D_e >> 1.
The magnetic equilibrium was calculated self-consistently, and additional transport was added within the sawteeth inversion radius around ρ ~ 0.3.
The T_i/T_e ratio at the internal boundary condition (ρ=0.8) had a considerable impact on the density peaking predictions.
The simulations successfully reproduced the experimental temperature and density profiles, providing confidence that the correct ITG regime was being captured.
The model was able to quantitatively reproduce the experimental deuterium to electron density ratio, with only a slight overestimation for one pulse.
Tungsten (W) contribution to dilution and Z_eff was almost negligible in these discharges, so W was not included in the modeling.
Fast ion species were not included in the integrated modeling, as their impact was found to be negligible.
The pulses studied had plasma current I_p = 1.38 MA, magnetic field B_t = 1.7 T, and 8 MW of NBI heating power.
The edge composition was measured to have Z_eff around 1.15-1.2 for all discharges.
The experimental data were averaged for ~400 ms during flat-top, as defined by kinetic profile quasi-stationarity over several confinement times.
The simulations were constrained to the core, with a boundary condition taken at ρ = 0.8 from the Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) fit.
